title: The House of Wisdom
body: In ninth-century Baghdad the Abbasid caliphs gathered scholars of many faiths and languages and set them to translating the learning of Greece, Persia and India into Arabic. Tradition calls the place they worked the House of Wisdom. Medicine, astronomy, mathematics and philosophy all passed through it, and much of it reached Europe centuries later through those Arabic books. Notice what the story is made of: the roots you have just learned, for writing, reading and knowing.

title: Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves
body: A poor woodcutter hides in a tree and watches forty thieves ride up to a wall of rock. Their leader says two words, the rock opens, and they go in. When they have left, Ali Baba tries the words himself: "Open, O sesame!" The command is the root ف ت ح, opening, which you have just learned. The tale is one of the best-known of the Thousand and One Nights; it was told to the French translator Antoine Galland by a Syrian storyteller, Hanna Diyab.

title: Scheherazade
body: King Shahryar, betrayed by his wife, takes a new bride each day and has her killed the next morning. Scheherazade, the vizier's daughter, offers to marry him. That night she begins a story and stops at dawn with the ending untold. The king spares her to hear it, and the next night she finishes it and starts another. This goes on for a thousand and one nights, by which time he has given up his vow. The whole collection, "A Thousand Nights and a Night", hangs on that frame: a life saved by telling.

title: Layla and Majnun
body: Qays and Layla grow up together and fall in love. Qays makes poems about her so openly that her family, shamed, refuses him and marries her to another man. He wanders into the desert, living among the animals and reciting her name, and people start calling him Majnūn: the one possessed, the madman. His name is the pattern مَفْعُول, the one something has been done to. The story is told across the Arab world, Persia and beyond as the pattern of love that cannot be had.

title: The generosity of Hatim
body: Hatim of the tribe of Tayy, a poet who lived before Islam, is the Arab byword for open-handedness. In the best-known story, guests reach his tent in a year of famine when there is nothing left to cook. Rather than send them away hungry he slaughters his own horse, the most valuable thing he owns, and serves it to them. To this day, to call someone "more generous than Hatim" is the highest praise for a host. The phrase uses the pattern أَفْعَل: more, most.

title: Juha and the pot
body: Juha is the wise fool of Arab folklore, the hero of hundreds of short jokes. In one, he borrows a cooking pot from his neighbour and returns it with a smaller pot inside. "Your pot gave birth," he explains, and the neighbour happily keeps both. Later Juha borrows the pot again and does not bring it back. "I am sorry," he says, "your pot has died." The neighbour protests that a pot cannot die. "You believed it could give birth," says Juha.

title: Kalila and Dimna
body: Two jackals, Kalila and Dimna, live at the court of a lion king. Dimna is ambitious and schemes his way into the king's favour; Kalila warns him where it will end. Around their story are nested dozens of animal fables about how rulers should rule and how the powerless can survive them. The book began in India, passed into Persian, and was put into Arabic in the eighth century by Ibn al-Muqaffaʿ. His version became a model of Arabic prose and the source of most later translations.

title: Sindbad the Sailor
body: A rich merchant of Baghdad tells a poor porter how he came by his fortune: seven voyages, each ending in shipwreck and each stranger than the last. He lands on an island that turns out to be a sleeping whale, is carried off by the giant bird called the rukh, and escapes the Old Man of the Sea. His title in Arabic is al-Baḥrī, "of the sea": the word بَحْر with the ending that makes an adjective.

title: Zarqa al-Yamama
body: Zarqa, the blue-eyed woman of Yamama, could see a rider three days' journey away, and her tribe relied on her to warn them of raids. An enemy army, knowing this, cut down trees and marched behind the branches. Zarqa told her people that the trees were walking towards them. They laughed, and were overrun. Her name is still used for anyone who sees far and is not believed. You now have the words for what she saw: something far coming near.

title: Hayy ibn Yaqzan
body: A child grows up alone on an island, raised by a gazelle. When she dies he tries to find what has left her, and from that first question works his way, by observation and reasoning alone, through the nature of animals, the stars and finally the cause behind everything. Ibn Tufayl wrote the tale in twelfth-century al-Andalus as an argument that reason and revelation arrive at one truth. The hero's name means "Alive, son of Awake". Like him, you have been getting here one cause and one result at a time.

title: Ibn Sina and the Canon
body: Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, was born near Bukhara around 980 and was practising as a doctor while still in his teens. His great work, the Canon of Medicine, gathered what Greek, Persian, Indian and Arab physicians knew into one ordered system: how to examine a patient, how illnesses spread, how to test a remedy. Translated into Latin, it was a standard textbook in European universities for some five hundred years. Its title is two roots you now know: law, and medicine.

title: The travels of Ibn Battuta
body: In 1325 a young man of twenty-one left Tangier to make the pilgrimage to Mecca. He did not come home for twenty-four years. Ibn Battuta went on through Persia, down the coast of East Africa, across Central Asia to India, where he served as a judge, and on to China, then later across the Sahara to Mali. Back in Morocco he dictated what he had seen. The book is known simply as the Riḥla, the Journey: the word you have just learned.

title: Al-Khansa, poet of grief
body: Tumadir bint Amr, called al-Khansa, lived in Arabia in the seventh century. When her brothers Muawiya and Sakhr were killed in tribal fighting she mourned them, Sakhr above all, in elegies of such force that she became the most celebrated woman poet in Arabic. Tradition says the Prophet Muhammad liked to hear her recite. Her poems turn on the two words this campaign set side by side: sorrow, and the patience that outlasts it.

title: The man who tried to fly
body: Abbas ibn Firnas was an inventor and poet in ninth-century Cordoba, who made lenses and a water clock and built a model of the heavens in his house. The story told of him is that, already an old man, he covered a frame with feathers, climbed a height outside the city and jumped. He glided some way before coming down hard and hurting his back; later writers said he had forgotten that birds land on their tails. Whether it happened just so, he is remembered for the attempt.

title: The City of Peace
body: In 762 the caliph al-Mansur chose a site on the Tigris and had a new capital laid out as a perfect circle: ring walls, four gates facing the four directions, and at the centre the palace and the great mosque. He named it Madinat as-Salam, the City of Peace, though everyone went on using the older name of the place, Baghdad. Within a century it was among the largest cities in the world, and home to the House of Wisdom where your first story began.
